relevance_reason: Reports 7 patients with a novel milder TBCE phenotype (amyotrophy, testicular failure) caused by the c.100+1G>A variant, matching this entry's subject.

findings.statement: Sparber et al. (2025) reported 7 patients with a novel, milder TBCE-associated phenotype presenting with amyotrophy, testicular failure, and mild intellectual disability, with or without short stature. Electron microscopy showed varying levels of acto-myosin degradation.
quotes: We report 7 patients with a novel, milder TBCE phenotype, presenting with amyotrophy, testicular failure, and mild intellectual disability, with or without short stature.
Electron microscopy revealed varying levels of acto-myosin degradation.

findings.statement: In 7 patients with a milder TBCE-related phenotype, Sparber et al. (2025) identified homozygosity or compound heterozygosity for a splice site variant in the TBCE gene (NM_003193.5:c.100+1G>A) that causes a splicing alteration and early frameshift, as shown by deep sequencing of RT-PCR products.
quotes: All patients were homozygous or compound-heterozygous for the NM_003193.5:c.100 + 1G > A variant, which causes a splicing alteration and early frameshift.

findings.statement: Sparber et al. (2025) found that the mild phenotype associated with the TBCE c.100+1G>A variant arises from translation from an alternative open reading frame, producing a partially functional protein. Patient dermal fibroblasts showed reduced Golgi compactness but normal microtubule dynamics.
quotes: However, we found that the mild phenotype arises due to translation from an alternative open reading frame, producing a partially functional protein.
Dermal fibroblasts showed reduced Golgi compactness but normal microtubule dynamics.

findings.statement: Sparber et al. (2025) found the TBCE c.100+1G>A variant to be 10 times more frequent in Slavic samples than in gnomAD, suggesting underdiagnosis of this phenotype.
quotes: The c.100 + 1G > A variant was found to be 10 times more frequent in Slavic samples than in gnomAD, suggesting underdiagnosis of this phenotype.

relevance_reason: Reports three patients homozygous for TBCE c.100+1G>A who have rigid spine, scoliosis, myopathy and cryptorchidism/testicular atrophy in males, which is the phenotype this entry covers.

findings.statement: Badura-Stronka et al. (2025) reported a 13-year-old Polish girl (P1) with no significant family history. She was born at term with normal birth weight, walked independently at 14 months and had slight speech delay. At age 6 she developed muscle weakness and limited cervical spine mobility with increased paraspinal muscle tone. The rigid spine progressed to involve the thoracic and lumbar segments, and thoracic scoliosis worsened from age 11. At 13 she had proximal muscle weakness, limb muscle atrophy, diminished tendon reflexes, waddling gait, weight and height below the 3rd percentile, and nocturnal hypoxemia with central and obstructive apneas that required nocturnal noninvasive ventilation. She also had osteoporosis (T-score -3.9), eosinophilia, neutropenia and platelet anisocytosis.
quotes: The initial symptoms manifested at age 6, presenting as muscle weakness and limited mobility in the cervical spine. Increased muscle tone around the paraspinal muscles was noted. Over the subsequent years, the symptoms of a rigid spine progressed, involving both the thoracic and lumbar segments.

A neurological examination at age 13 revealed reduced muscle strength in proximal muscles, atrophy of limb muscles, diminished tendon reflexes, and waddling gait. Body weight and height were below the 3rd percentile. Nocturnal hypoxemia was noted.

Additionally, densitometry results indicated osteoporosis (Z-score − 1.5, T-score − 3.9), and blood serum analysis revealed eosinophilia, neutropenia, and platelet anisocytosis (without thrombocytopenia).

findings.statement: Badura-Stronka et al. (2025) reported a 20-year-old Polish man (P2) with bilateral cryptorchidism, mildly delayed motor and speech development, febrile seizures from age 4 during recurrent pneumonia, and generalized muscle pain from age 5. At 11 he had contractures and distal limb paresis, and muscle biopsy showed mild, nonspecific myopathic changes. From 13 he had limited spine mobility, shoulder girdle atrophy and nocturnal hypoxemia that required noninvasive ventilation. MRI showed atrophy and fatty infiltration of the paraspinal, iliopsoas, gluteal and thigh muscles. He also had gynecomastia at 14, thoracic scoliosis, strabismus, a high palate, an inability to flex the thoracic and lumbar spine, and persistent eosinophilia and neutropenia from age 10. EMG showed moderate myogenic features.
quotes: Bilateral cryptorchidism was noted. Motor development occurred with discrete delay, achieving independent sitting at 9 months and independent walking at 15 months.
Subsequent neurological evaluation at the age of 13 revealed limited spine mobility, muscle atrophy primarily affecting the shoulder girdle, and the onset of nocturnal hypoxemia events.
At 14, gynecomastia and abnormal densitometry results (Z-score 0.3, T-score − 1.5) were observed.
Due to the rigidity of the paraspinal muscles, the patient cannot flex the thoracic and lumbar spine. Eosinophilia and neutropenia were consistently observed over 10 years (from age 10).

phenotypes.text: paraspinal muscle atrophy and fatty infiltration

phenotypes.hpo_label: Febrile seizure (within the age range of 3 months to 6 years)

findings.statement: Badura-Stronka et al. (2025) reported an 18-year-old Ukrainian man (P3) with bilateral inguinal cryptorchidism, treated by orchidopexy at ages 3 and 4. He had recurrent respiratory infections, otitis and bronchitis from age 3. He underwent gonadectomy at ages 10 and 15, and histology showed atrophic and sclerotic testes with no spermatogenesis. He had intellectual disability, dysmorphic features and neutropenia, but motor development was normal.
quotes: Bilateral inguinal cryptorchidism was noted—orchidopexy was performed at the age of 3 and 4. Motor development was normal.

The patient underwent a gonadectomy of the first testicle at the age of 10 and the second one at the age of 15; the histological report confirmed atrophic and sclerotic changes in the testicles and no signs of spermatogenesis.
The patient was diagnosed with intellectual disability.

findings.statement: In 3 patients (2 Polish and 1 Ukrainian), Badura-Stronka et al. (2025) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a homozygous splice-site variant in the TBCE gene (c.100+1G>A) affecting the intron 2 donor splice site. All parents were confirmed to be heterozygous carriers. The variant had conflicting pathogenicity classifications in ClinVar and had not previously been reported in patients.
quotes: A homozygous pathogenic variant c.100 + 1G > A in TBCE was detected in three patients (P1-P3), followed by the confirmation of heterozygous carrier status of the variant in their parents.
In the c.100 + 1G > A variant, the sequence alteration impacts a donor splice site within intron 2 of the TBCE, potentially disrupting RNA splicing.

The ClinVar database provides information about conflicting pathogenicity classifications for this variant based on current submissions from genetic laboratories: pathogenic (2), likely pathogenic (3), uncertain significance (1).

findings.statement: From a systematic review of 98 previously reported TBCE patients plus their own 3, Badura-Stronka et al. (2025) concluded that homozygosity for c.100+1G>A causes a milder course than other TBCE variants. These patients had later onset (mean age 5 years), normal motor development, eventual normal speech, normal calcium-phosphate metabolism and no significant CNS MRI changes. Distinctive features included cryptorchidism in males, rigid spine, proximal muscle atrophy, scoliosis, neutropenia, eosinophilia and nocturnal hypoxemia. By contrast, patients homozygous for c.155_166del had the HRDS/KCS1 phenotype, and those with c.464T>A had severe neurodevelopmental disease without genital abnormalities.
quotes: Homozygous carriers of the c.100 + 1G > A variant exhibit a markedly milder clinical course, with no deviations in the calcium-phosphate metabolism and central nervous system pathology in MRI studies.
Bilateral cryptorchidism was observed in both male patients—a trait absent in all (5/5) male carriers of c.464 T > A variants.

The primary clinical differences compared to homozygous c.464 T > A individuals include the onset of symptoms at a later developmental stage, normal motor development, eventual proper speech development, and cryptorchidism in boys.

findings.statement: Badura-Stronka et al. (2025) noted that the c.100+1G>A TBCE variant had so far been found only in patients of Central-Eastern European descent, and they suggested it may be a founder mutation in this population.
quotes: The identification of the pathogenic c.100 + 1G > A variant has thus far been limited to patients of Central-Eastern European descent, suggesting a potential founder mutation in this population.
